newsitem.title: CONGO: Red Cross calls off body mission in tense Congo.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross calls off body mission in tense Congo.

text.p: Congo's warring leaders backed a planned U.N. force to cement their truce on Sunday but the Red Cross was forced to abandon a mission to bury hundreds of dead in the tense capital, Brazzaville.

"We are all agreed that a pan-African force should come to intervene and to help us secure elections," said Bernard Kolelas, mayor of Brazzaville, the capital that fighting this month has split into rival camps.

Kolelas is leading a local mediation team that includes representatives of President Pascal Lissouba and his rival, former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso. All three were hopefuls in postponed July presidential elections.
The U.N. Security Council authorised Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Saturday to sound out mainly African countries about contributing to a force of 1,600 to 1,800 soldiers.
Ignoring a U.N. plea for 1,250 French troops to stay, Paris pulled them out last week after they had finished evacuating foreign residents, and the truce has frayed at the edges since.
Gunfire and occasional shells disturbed the Sunday lie-in of citizens who, if they were lucky, have managed to flee the disputed centre of town to safer outlying areas.

Calm reigned for most of the rest of the day, but the international Red Cross (ICRC) said the central no-man's-land and the frontline areas were so tense that they were suspending a mission to collect bodies.
"There is no way we are going to lose a live person for a dead body," said ICRC spokesman Darcy Christen, whose teams dodged sniping and crossfire to retrieve some 100 bodies over the weekend.
He said another 100-200 bodies, rotting where they were shot down, would have to wait until it was safer.
The death toll from fighting that began on June 5 is estimated at up to 1,000. Some were buried earlier on, others dumped in the mighty Congo river that flows beside the city.
Fighting began when Lissouba tried to disarm the Cobra militia of Sassou, a Marxist turned capitalist who ruled for 13 years until free elections in 1992 brought Lissouba to power.
Kolelas blamed "tired and nervous" rogue elements on both sides for weekend violations in the ceasefire that is due to last until next weekend.
French envoy Raymond Cesaire, the only ambassador left in Paris' former colony, continued his shuttle diplomacy on Sunday between Lissouba and Sassou, protected by 30 French gendarmes.
"There has been no real progress," said his adviser, Laurent Viguier. "It's very difficult to make progress here."
The Security Council said any intervention force depended on a solid truce and proof of a will by both sides to find a political solution.

A similar African contingent in the mutiny-prone Central African Republic next door was caught up in fresh fighting at the weekend, an inauspicious sign for attempts to recruit a new force for Brazzaville.
International mediation efforts led by President Omar Bongo of neighbouring Gabon are due to resume next week.
